314	An effective reproach in addressing our theoreticians is to remember that the pathway to using 
315	knowledge of laws of adaptation of man to conditions of sports activity were concretely formed 
316	by N.N. Yakovlev even 40 years ago and were further defined in the articles, “The significance 
317	of disturbed homeostasis for effectiveness of the training process" (1971) “Perspectives in devel­
318	opment of sports biochemistry and their significance for sports practice" (1972) and “In order to 
319	successfully direct it is necessary to know the mechanisms’ (1976).
320	According to Yakovlev, practical tasks in the biochemistry of sport, orientated to the study of 
321	applied problems of adaptation of man to loaded (sports) muscle activity, can be formulated into 
322	three points:
323	1. Finding ways of increasing the intensity of the adaptational changes in the highly trained 
324	body;
325	2. Finding ways of speeding up biochemical restitution;
326	3. Finding biochemical tests to evaluate trainedness in speed-strength and technical type sports.
327	In resolving the first task, it appears to be rational to proceed from the level of disturbance of the 
328	biochemical homeostasis during execution of the training loads. With an increase in trainedncss 
329	this disturbance decreases, and the less it becomes, the less are the following consequences re­
330	maining from the muscular activity and that lie in the base of adaptation. Because of this, with 
331	an increase in trainedness, it becomes inevitable that the training loads should increase.
332	However, on the contemporary stage of sports development we cannot practically further in­
333	crease the intensity and duration of the training loads without harming the body. A more realistic 
334	path here is to find supplementary factors that bring about disturbance of the homeostasis similar 
335	to those that are observed during muscular activity. As a result, this means strengthening the fol­
336	lowing consequent appearances, left by the latter.
337	Resolution of the second task, speeding up restoration, should go along the pathway of further 
338	effective nutrition for the athletes and the use of physical factors: massage, hydro procedures and 
339	physiotherapy.
340	The third task is the most difficult. What can help to some extent is the study of the ATP bal­
341	ance in the working muscles. For this it follows to add that the practical methods of experimen­
342	tally studying the problems of adaptation should be based mainly on the study of the tendencies 
343	(laws) in the dynamics of the athletes state during long term stages of preparation in relation to 
344	the training loads executed (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, Verkhoshansky et al. 22, 279).
345	With sorrow, these recommendations were not heard (more precisely, not understood) by the 
346	apologists for the conception of Periodization of training, that over the last 10 years has held 
347	back development of the scientific bases in the theory and methods of sports training.
348	Great hope is laid on the science of man for the theory of adaptation. It appears very possible that 
349	in the near future, according to the accumulation of knowledge, attention of investigators will be 
350	re-oriented toward more simple registration of the dynamics of the functional state in the process 
351	of accommodation of the body to the surroundings and activity directing adaptation (Meerson, 
352	76, 77, Medvedev, 73).

359	1) the optimal regimes of influencing the adaptive factor,
360	2) non-specific methods of increasing physical workability

362	The aim of such a complex approach will speed up the accommodative process, decrease its phy­
363	siological and psychological cost, lengthen the period during which the state of adaptation is

Based on all the material looked at above, it is possible to conclude that the process of adaptation 
during sports activity is characterized by a constant system-discreet influences of the adaptogenic 
factor on the body, ensuring progressive improvement (development) of his specific motor abili­
ties. This means that the adaptation factor function is not permanent (as let us say in adaptation
542


######## PDF 554 / p.543
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
to climatic-geographical conditions), but is repeated with a definite periodicity (systematically) 
in time. Between the adaptogenic factor influences, developed by their activation, is the accom­
modative restructuring (change) in the body, of converted, discreet influences in a steady (un­
broken) flow of a continuous process that is progressively developed.
In this way, on the basis of the material looked at above, long term adaptation to sports activity 
can be presented as an uninterrupted cyclical changing event, tied in with exhaustion and restora­
tion of CAR in the body. Moving away from here, the morpho-functional acquisition carries a 
definite qualitative and quantitative change in the complex of external and internal relationships 
in the body. This ensures a higher level of specialized workability of the athlete and greater pro­
gress in his mastery'.
It is correct to propose that this process develops both vertically as well as horizontally (Verkho­
shansky, Viru, 28, 286). In other words, the accommodative restructurings have a concrete level 
of structure, functioning within the limits of definite segments (phases) of coordinated time (Fig­
ure 15).
The process of adaptation begins with activation of specific homeostatic reactions (first level of 
adaptation). Repeat shifts in constant internal surroundings in the body and strengthening the re­
serves of energy and plastic provision brings about activation of non-specific mechanisms of ad­
aptation and transition to compensatory adaptation (second level).
The mechanism of compensatory adaptation provides relatively stoic morpho-functional im­
provement in the cellular structure, which appears as an unchanging condition for development 
of long term adaptation, transforming the body into a new, higher level of specialized capabilities 
(third level).
Figure 15 - The structure of the process of long-term adaptation to the intensive muscular work
543


######## PDF 555 / p.544
S UPERTRA IN INC ADDENDUM
Thus, compensatory adaptation is an intermediate link between short term and steady accommo­
dative reactions, creating an objectively necessary level for the following repeat activation of 
specific homeostatic reactions and for temporary redistribution of the plastic reserves of the 
body.
From here, it follows that long term adaptation (during sports activity) is a phasic multi-step ac­
cumulation process. It is developed on the multiple short term repetition mechanism of compen­
satory adaptation and periodic deductions in the fund of stabilized steady accommodative re­
structuring of morpho-functional “surpluses”, acquired by the body on the hemeostatic and non­
specific reaction level.
Studies in multiple sports (Viru, 32, Kassil et al. 61, Verkhoshansky, 20, 24, 25) substantiate the 
correctness of the theoretical positions used in the above schemes of compensatory and long term 
adaptation. Their results and principal positions and the methodological recommendations result­
ing from them touching on programming and organization of the training process, has found 
wide use in practice (Verkhoshansky, 26, 27).
The studied laws of long term adaptation have serious practical significance, that is, they defi­
nitely show the criteria for rational organization of the multiyear training process that can ensure 
favorable conditions for effective realization of the laws of adaptation of the body to a loaded 
regime of muscular activity.
CONCLUSIONS
Applied aspects of the problem
Concrete ways of using objective knowledge of the laws of adaptation of man in sports practice 
during loaded muscular activity, have frequently been looked at in the literature. It follows first 
of all to recall the fundamental research by N.N.Yakovlev (137, 140, 144), A.A. Viru (32, 289, 
291) and G. N. Kassil (60, 61, 62). With sorrow, this knowledge, as with many fundamental and 
applied studies in the area of physiology and biochemistry of muscle activity, was not used to the 
fullest extent by noted theoreticians for deepening and developing the theory and methods of 
sports training.
Two ways have been determined to reorganize contemporary theory and methods of sports train­
ing based on the content and laws of development of adaptation of mans' body to loaded muscle 
activity.
One of them is related to the principle of constructing the training and is directly tied in with the 
mechanism of compensatory adaptation and understanding the large (macro) training cycle.
The large training cycle is principally a new form of organizing the training process in the theory 
of sport. It is tied in with the aim of realizing CAR of the athletes body (Verkhoshansky 24 - 27, 
Verkhoshansky, Viru, 28, 286).
This form has already outlived the period of the “orientational reflex" from the side of specialists 
and is finding wider use in sports practice.
544


######## PDF 556 / p.545
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
The second problem (way) is tied in with the mechanism of short term adaptation. It is definitely 
related to such organizational-time forms of constructing the training process such as the micro­
cycle, training day and training seance18 (for details see Verkhoshansky, 24 - 27).
Today, both of these problems have priority significance for further development of the scientific 
bases of the theory and methods of sports training.
The first of them has already received plenty of substantial evaluation. The second is not consid­
ered as only a single study - even though it is sufficiently prospective. Related to it first of all, 
are studies carried out using of biochemical methods (Viru, Kirge, 35, Viru, 291, Verkho­
shansky, 27, Bereznoy 5, Dahnovsky et al, 47, Eepik, 135, Eepik, Viru, 136, Osoliny et al, 92, 
Usik et al 118).
The principal approach to the organization of the large training cycle presented in Figure 16. The 
level of specific workability of the athlete (B) is determined mainly by two factors: strength of 
the training influence (A) and volume of CAR (the abscissa) or more precisely the level at which 
it can be withstood. The increase in specific workability according to the degree of withstanding 
CAR, requires accelerated growth of a stronger training influence. In practice this is expedient 
and proven only up to the moment of entering onto the plateau level of specialized workability of 
the athlete (B) because of the maximal loading function. Further on. if the limit loading function 
is allowed, it is followed by a non optimal form of a training load effect, indices of specific 
workability begin to decrease (Volkov, 38).
This moment can be looked at as evidence of the exhaustion of the “allowable” (according to 
Hollmann, Hettinger, 218) physiological reserves, that in reality have a place in rationally organ­
ized training (Verkhoshansky, 24, 281, 282, 283, 294, 295). It is possible to further propose that
Figure 16 - The principal scheme of the relationship between the dynamic of the athlete state (B) and the magnitude 
of the training impact (A) and the level of the CAR exhaustion (Y. Verkhoshansky, 1993)
A training seance or TS (from the French “seance", the interval of time covering the non-interrupted perform­
ance of work or process in training session) ) is the form of rationalizing a one-time portion of the training load, 
intended to achieve one specific target (to improve the athletes' sportsmanship tactics and strategy or special 
physical training)
545


######## PDF 557 / p.546
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
the remaining part of CAR of the body presents itself as a so-called “automatic defense work re­
serve" (according to Hollman, Hettinger, 218), comprising about 30% of CAR. Realization of 
this part of CAR with a high functional effect is mainly possible during stressful situations or 
because of extreme load intensification and doping. However, in conditions of natural training 
this is intolerable as it threatens to derange adaptation and have heavier consequences on the 
body.
Two indisputable conditions should be observed in the organization of the large training cycle: 
First, concrete purposes for the training load (the physiological and energy systems, their mecha­
nisms and functional properties) and the clearness of presenting the training task (what is defi­
nitely required be achieved). Because of this, in the selection and organization of training loads, 
it is necessary to proceed first of all from knowledge of the functional capabilities of the physio­
logical and energy systems, which primarily provide the athletes specific workability. Second, 
should be about their adaptational inertness according to the other systems and third, the hetero­
chronicity of development of the adaptational reactions on the level of different life providing 
systems of the body in the course of the training process (Verkhoshansky, 24, 281, 282, 294, 
295).
Illustration of these conditions in the cyclical type sports is presented in Figure 17.
The schematic shows the temporary structure of the entire direction that entails the complex of 
training influences on the functional parameters of the cardio-vascular (CV) system and the neu- 
ro-muscular system (NM) in the general orientational strategy of the training to gradually in­
crease distance speed in the competitive exercise (V). The idea for such a structure is in the fol­
lowing (Verkhoshansky, 25, 26, 27, 283, 285):
a) 
On the CV level, the training effect at the beginning (stage A) is simultaneously directed to 
an increase in the heart volume (dilation) and formation of peripheral blood vessel reac­
tions (distribution of the circulatory network) and after this to raising the minute volume of 
the blood by increasing in the power of the myocardium (stage B) and heart contraction 
frequency (stage C):
b) 
On the level of the NM system, there are simultaneous increases in the contractile proper­
ties of the muscles and the start of perfecting the oxidative properties of the slow twitch 
(stage A), and after this, fast twitch (stage B) muscle fibers. On stage C there is an in­
crease in the power of the muscular system work in specific cyclical regimes;
c) 
Along the vertical (corresponding to stages A, B, C) it is easy to trace the entailment of the 
training affects on the CV system (specific distance) and on the NM system (by means of 
SPP —specialized physical preparation). It should be emphasized that the means of SPP 
includes specialized strength exercises which includes exercises with weights. However, 
their task is in the development of not only just strength, but local muscular endurance 
(LME) primarily of the muscle groups used (Verkhoshansky, 25, 27 295).
The structure of the training effects that were looked at are in agreement with the performed 
functions of the muscular, vegetative, energy and hormonal systems of the body that are em­
ployed in the speed regime of distance work, that requires endurance. Also realized is the princi­
ple of the “anti glycolytic direction” of training and superimposition of loads having a primary 
direction (Verkhoshansky. 25,26).
546


######## PDF 558 / p.547
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
The model of the large training cycle reflects the principle (strategic) idea of its organization for 
high level athletes irrespective of concrete times and the calendar of competitions. In practice, 
this idea should be used creatively, taking into consideration the motor specifics in each sport 
and the calendar and regularity of competitions.
Figure 17 - The schematic structure of the training loads temporal organization during the subsequent stages 
A, B and C of the Large Training Stage.
On the graphic above: the curve of the total volume of the training loads (the curves A, B. C represent only the 
loads with different emphasis but not their volume).
The schemes under the graphic represents the sequence of introductions in training process of the training 
loads having the primarily directions to the improvement of different parameters of the Cardiovascular system 
and the Neuromuscular system.
547

Further perspectives in the use of the theory of adaptation in sports practice
"In order to successfully manage, it is necessary to know the mechanisms "
N.N. Yakovlev
In our time we are seeing the compilation of fundamental scientific theory of sports training. 
Some of the more quality prerequisites for its formation are:
1. 
Experimental achievements in the biological sciences, biomechanics of physical exercises, 
physiology and biochemistry of muscular activity.
2. 
Accumulation of objective medical-biological and methodological information, relative to 
the conceptions, principles, methods and trials of preparation of outstanding and foreign 
high level athletes, including professional.
3. 
Scientific cultivation of effective methods of psycho-pedagogical influences on the athlete 
in the process of training and competitive activity, and in post and inter-competitive periods.
The priority of biologically composed information in the formation of ideas and content of con­
temporary theory and methods of sports training is not by chance. In the last two decades the 
biological sciences have substantially enriched the functional picture of body function during 
loaded sports activity. And if in past years these sciences supplied only the essentials of the the­
ory and methods of sports training and were enlisted only for “substantiation** of its principles 
that were formed on an empirical base, then now they are used in a prognostic function. And if 
one is to speak seriously of the scientific bases of the theory and methods of sports training, then 
it is difficult to say which of these is now greater, the pedagogical or the biological.
The need on the level of and reliability of the preparation of high level athletes has grown im­
measurably. The large volume of training and competitive loads and the increasing struggle with 
the use of biologically active preparations have served in the latter years to increase the interest 
in searching for new pathways in the theory and methods of training (Verkhoshansky, 26). In 
doing this specialists are frequently forced to doubt and with all their power, overcome their spe­
culative pseudo-pedagogical concepts of training and with trust, turn to the biological sciences.
Today it is obvious that in the area of biological knowledge these hopes are tied in with the ath­
lete’s adaptation to loaded muscular activity. This is undoubtedly justified, if the word ‘"adapta­
tion" is not used simply as advertisement for publication, containing an account of trivial sports 
training questions19. Secondly, if the understanding of adaptation is not made to fit under the an­
tiquated principles of training with the aim of reanimating the latter and is not limited to trials 
with speculative forms “put together” of the theory of training and the theory of adaptation"20.
The theory of training should not be at odds with the theory of adaptation, but be based on its 
positions. It should be possible to methodologically analyze the adaptation process and write, 
not according to the dynamics of sports results or phases of establishing notorious “sports
See for example V.N.Platonov. Adaptation in sport. Health, Kiev 1988,215pg.
20 L.P. Matveev, F.Z.Meerson. Principles of the theory of training and competition in the theory of adaptation to 
physical loads. In the book. Essays on the theory of physical culture (Moscow,. Physical culture and sport, 1984, 
pp 224-240.
548


######## PDF 560 / p.549
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
form"21, but by the dynamics of the physiological state of the body, that determine the compati­
bility of the influences of the training loads and their organization according to time (Verkho­
shansky, 26, 27).
It is necessary to emphasize that the free treatment of the word “adaptation" is characteristic not 
only in the area of sports science. Widely spread is the idea, in agreement with which is any 
change that takes place in the body of man and in animals, is the result of being in a non-optimal 
condition, is known as adaptive. The term “adaptation" is used in many cases for explaining the 
processes which do not accompany adaptive restructuring, but in the process of evolution of al­
ready formed mechanisms (Haydarliu, 124, Medvedev, 73). In the foundation of these processes 
are the physiological-biochemical reactions with no restructuring of the hemeostatic mechanisms 
or loading in the functions of separate organs and systems for achieving the usual “adaptation”. 
The surrounding conditions, in which similar changes take place, appear to be adequate as the 
body is adapted to them, and “any display of life activity of the body to adequate conditions can­
not be considered “adaptive” (Kaznacheev, 59). Nonetheless, this terminology easily became 
customary.
However, it is always necessary to recall that such views of reactions cannot be carried over to 
true adaptation (Haydarliu, 124). The need for adaptation to occur in conditions of sports activity 
is when the parameters of external and internal interactions of the athletes body change to such a 
degree, that they cease to be adequate for his current functional capabilities (Verkhoshansky, Vi­
ru, 28, 286, Viru, 291).
The theory of adaptation plays its methodological and scientific-practical role in the theory and 
methods and sports training only in those cases if attention to it is concentrated not on the phe­
nomena (external side), but on its physiological mechanism. Because of this, today, in the theory 
and methods and sports training, it is extremely useful to have explanation of the results of ex­
perimental studies characterizing not only, and not so much, the external side of the adaptation 
process, that is, the functional and morpho-functional provision of the body or its separate 
physiological systems as result of one or another regime of muscular activity, including sports 
activity, (Verkhoshansky, 24,25, Pshennikova,99, Yakovlev. 144 ) but in its main form that stud­
ies the hormonal mechanisms of the non-specific component of long term adaptation of the body 
to loaded muscular activity (Meerson, Pshennikova, 78, Viru, 32, 291).
However, an especially important applied value that will be gotten from investigations oriented 
to the study of not only the results, but the process of long term adaptation to sports activity, its 
concrete quantitative-temporal parameters (Verkhoshansky, 21, 25, 26,27, 285, Verkhoshansky. 
Viru, 28, 286) and frequently the laws of morphofunctional specialization of the athlete's body in 
the process of multi-year training (Verkhoshansky, 17, 24, 293) and tendencies in the dynamic 
state of the athletes in the yearly cycle under the influence of the given training loads (Verkho­
shansky et al 22, 279).
21 Unluckily, in the conception of Periodization of training, the meaning of the term “sport form" was interpreted 
as the level of “preparedness”, i.e. the stable level of adaptation of the athlete’s body, and after, was assimilated 
with the meaning of the term “sport result”, i.e., level of performance. The original meaning of this term, intro­
duced by L. Prokop as the best current “readiness” of the athlete's body to carry out the competition activity, was 
ignored in this interpretation.
549


######## PDF 561 / p.550
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
An effective reproach in addressing our theoreticians is to remember that the pathway to using 
knowledge of laws of adaptation of man to conditions of sports activity were concretely formed 
by N.N. Yakovlev even 40 years ago and were further defined in the articles, “The significance 
of disturbed homeostasis for effectiveness of the training process" (1971) “Perspectives in devel­
opment of sports biochemistry and their significance for sports practice" (1972) and “In order to 
successfully direct it is necessary to know the mechanisms’ (1976).
According to Yakovlev, practical tasks in the biochemistry of sport, orientated to the study of 
applied problems of adaptation of man to loaded (sports) muscle activity, can be formulated into 
three points:
1. Finding ways of increasing the intensity of the adaptational changes in the highly trained 
body;
2. Finding ways of speeding up biochemical restitution;
3. Finding biochemical tests to evaluate trainedness in speed-strength and technical type sports.
In resolving the first task, it appears to be rational to proceed from the level of disturbance of the 
biochemical homeostasis during execution of the training loads. With an increase in trainedncss 
this disturbance decreases, and the less it becomes, the less are the following consequences re­
maining from the muscular activity and that lie in the base of adaptation. Because of this, with 
an increase in trainedness, it becomes inevitable that the training loads should increase.
However, on the contemporary stage of sports development we cannot practically further in­
crease the intensity and duration of the training loads without harming the body. A more realistic 
path here is to find supplementary factors that bring about disturbance of the homeostasis similar 
to those that are observed during muscular activity. As a result, this means strengthening the fol­
lowing consequent appearances, left by the latter.
Resolution of the second task, speeding up restoration, should go along the pathway of further 
effective nutrition for the athletes and the use of physical factors: massage, hydro procedures and 
physiotherapy.
The third task is the most difficult. What can help to some extent is the study of the ATP bal­
ance in the working muscles. For this it follows to add that the practical methods of experimen­
tally studying the problems of adaptation should be based mainly on the study of the tendencies 
(laws) in the dynamics of the athletes state during long term stages of preparation in relation to 
the training loads executed (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, Verkhoshansky et al. 22, 279).
With sorrow, these recommendations were not heard (more precisely, not understood) by the 
apologists for the conception of Periodization of training, that over the last 10 years has held 
back development of the scientific bases in the theory and methods of sports training.
Great hope is laid on the science of man for the theory of adaptation. It appears very possible that 
in the near future, according to the accumulation of knowledge, attention of investigators will be 
re-oriented toward more simple registration of the dynamics of the functional state in the process 
of accommodation of the body to the surroundings and activity directing adaptation (Meerson, 
76, 77, Medvedev, 73).
550


######## PDF 562 / p.551
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
Such directing, apparently, will become possible as a result of uniting:
1) the optimal regimes of influencing the adaptive factor,
2) non-specific methods of increasing physical workability
3) the selection of people, most adaptable to the influence of the adaptive factor.
The aim of such a complex approach will speed up the accommodative process, decrease its phy­
siological and psychological cost, lengthen the period during which the state of adaptation is 
maintained, and increase the economic effectiveness of the methods of adaptation used (Medve­
dev, 73, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286).
Today it is necessary to have scientific erudition and experimental-theoretical unification to seri­
ously resolve this problem.

# Small, Familiar Loads Stay Within Specific Homeostatic Reactions; Larger or Longer Loads Switch On the General (Stress) Adaptation Mechanism (Viru, Fig 2)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky, using Viru's scheme (9.1 Introduction, PDF 518-519 / p.507-508, checked against the page images): "Management of the adaptation process is done by the CNS (Figure 2)." Its first result is "the activation of specific homeostatic reactions." "When the strength (level) of the irritants is not high and the changes in the external and internal environment is not great, and in the presence of the previously worked out adaptation to a given action, the adaptational effect is limited to the specifics of the homeostatic reactions." As the strength and duration of the influence rise, the cells' own energy and plastic capabilities "require support from the side of general mobilization of the energy and plastic reserves of the body. This means mobilization of the non-specific component of adaptation or (according to Viru) inclusion of the general adaptation mechanism.

**Why it works** — The hormonal division of labour he gives, citing Viru (32, 289) and Yakovlev (144): "In mobilization of the energy resources of the body and in the energy provision function, predominant importance is given to the sympatho-adrenal system," acting through "hormonal (adrenaline) and mediatory (noradrenaline) links." "Mobilization of the plastic reserve of the body under stress is a function of the hypophyseal-adrenocortical system," tied to "the creation of a free amino acid reserve" for adaptive protein synthesis (PDF 519 / p.508). In the adapted body "there is increased power of the mechanism of the hormonal - humoral regulation," which "increases the maximum reaction of the body to limit loads, that ensures maximum mobilization of its functional capabilities" (PDF 519 / p.508).

**When to apply** — Inference: use the two branches to judge what a session asks for. A familiar, moderate session in a trained athlete stays in the specific branch and mostly maintains; a new, heavier or longer load recruits the general stress response, which is what funds new structure. This frames why Verkhoshansky ties progressive adaptation to a training influence that "brings about systematic disturbance of body homeostasis" (PDF 521 / p.510; see [[claim--compensatory-adaptation-is-temporary-and-precedes-stable-adaptation]]).

**When NOT to apply** — The page gives no thresholds: "not high" and "not great" are not quantified, so the scheme cannot tell a coach where one branch ends. It is a cited model (Viru 1981), shown without data, so it is rated `untested`. The stress-state framing follows Selye (cited on PDF 516), so the same caution applies as in the 8.5 overtraining entry: "stress" here is a whole-body hormonal state, not only fatigue. Inference: modern work adds local signalling (mechanical tension, for example) that this hormone-centred scheme does not show.

**Example** — Fig 2 (PDF 518 / p.507): the stressor reaches the CNS, which can answer through the specific homeostatic box alone or also through the three general-adaptation boxes, one of which leads on to "Ensuring the transition to the long term adaptation."

**Related** — [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]], [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]] (the same two hormonal systems cap the reserve), [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]] (8.5, Selye's stress), [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]] (6.9.4, the same specific-to-general-to-long-term sequence: "the fundamental condition for switching from the acute (specific) reaction ... to the general (non-specific) adaptive reaction, and then to the development of long-term adaptation", PDF 369 / p.358)

# Compensatory Adaptation Is Temporary and Comes First; Stable Adaptation Builds on It, and Has a Limit

**What it is** — The authors split adaptation into two layers (PDF p. 359 / printed p. 348, checked against the page image; the figure it refers to is on PDF p. 358):
- **Compensatory adaptation.** The annual changes in functional indicators (Fig 6.22, graphs B and C) "are temporary, unstable and to a certain extent, reversible." Their basis is "compensatory mechanisms, i.e. reactions designed to maintain the necessary level of functioning for brief periods under demanding conditions which ultimately lead to stable adaptation." These "gradually fade as adaptation takes place," and "Insofar as these mechanisms precede adaptation, they should be designated pre-adaptation phenomena (Kuznyetsov, 1979)."
- **Long-term, stable adaptation** (graph A). "compensatory adaptation is a prerequisite condition for the development of long-term, stable adaptation," which "can progressively increase if the functional reconstruction during the course of compensatory adaptation is sufficient to produce a noticeable effect on the external interactions of the body and increase its special work capacity."

Three further statements on the same page:
1. "adaptation cannot be considered an equilibrium process. Adaptation is the dynamic maintenance of a definite level of imbalance between the body and the environment" (Bauer, 1935; Bernstein, 1966).
2. The systems involved improve at different rates. This heterochronicity "is determined by: the action of particular physiological systems in establishing long-term adaptation of a specific emphasis; differences in their reactiveness (or adaptive inertia); changes in the role of these systems at different stages of long-term adaptation."
3. "Long-term compensatory adaptation cannot continue indefinitely." Its effect "diminishes with each repetition," described "by a parabola whose peak is eventually reached with time (Fig 6.22, graph A). This indicates that an athlete's general adaptation reserves have a limit that is genetically predetermined." The limit shows as "waves in the dynamics of special work capacity (graphs B and C)," caused partly by "traditional periodisation" but "a more important reason is the exhaustion of the so-called current adaptation reserves (CAR) of the body."

**Why it works** — The authors' account is the one above: short-term compensations hold function under stress, and if they change performance enough, the body consolidates them. They state that the picture is clearest in explosive-strength sports, and that research on adaptation (Folbrot, Selye) "has to be taken much further in its application to the development of sporting mastery, especially in endurance sports"; until then they assume "the same, above-mentioned chief mechanisms, although at another level of the physiological systems" (PDF p. 359 / printed p. 348). Inference: the "genetically predetermined" limit is inferred from the shape of the curve, not from genetic data.

**When to apply** — Inference: treat a season's gains in functional indicators as provisional until they hold through a lower-load period; a quality that survives the transition phase has become stable adaptation in the authors' terms. When a block stops producing gains, the authors' model points to exhausted current reserves before it points to a genetic ceiling (see [[principle--load-must-sit-within-the-current-adaptation-reserve-window]]).

**When NOT to apply** — No data are given for the parabola or the genetic limit. Graph A's slope shrinks each year, consistent with the parabola, but no peak is drawn within the three years (PDF p. 358 / printed p. 347). The "imbalance" definition is a theoretical position (Bauer, Bernstein), not a measured one. Inference: it is closer to the allostasis model in Evans's course material (regulation that changes set points to meet demand; see Related) than to fixed-set-point homeostasis.

**Example** — The authors' own: Fig 6.22, where the functional indicators B and C wave above and below the rising fitness state A within each year (PDF p. 358 / printed p. 347).

**Related** — [[claim--four-observations-on-long-term-speed-strength-adaptation]], [[principle--load-must-sit-within-the-current-adaptation-reserve-window]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[claim--heterochronic-biochemical-adaptation-sequence]], [[claim--heterochronicity-of-strength-quality-and-muscle-group-development-order]], [[claim--speed-barrier-is-genetic-ceiling-not-neural-block]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--homeostasis-vs-allostasis-mcewen-sterling]]. From 9.1: [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]] (9.1, the protein-synthesis mechanism of the transition), [[framework--bauer-kasnacheev-energy-and-plastic-flows-fig-1]].

**Also in 9.1** — Verkhoshansky's own paper restates the two layers in 9.1 §1.1, "Understanding compensatory adaptation" (PDF 521 / p.510, checked against the page image). The compensatory mechanisms are "dynamic and quickly rising physiological means of breakdown in order to provide for the body in extreme conditions and to gradually extinguish these means according to the amount of development of stable long term adaptation," so "they can be looked at as pre-adaptation appearances (Kusnetzov, 68)." Long-term adaptation "can have a progressive character if the training influence is stressful and brings about systematic disturbance of body homeostasis," and if the restructuring is "sufficiently substantial." # The Constructive Effect of Adaptation Has Three Bases and Works at Two Levels: Session Supercompensation and the Long-Term Delayed Training Effect

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.5, "Essentials of the constructive effects of the adaptational process," Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519, checked against the page image): "The foundation for the development of the adaptational process in sports activity is the strengthened synthesis of structural and enzymatic proteins in the actively functioning cells." Strengthened protein synthesis "appears as a constructive effect of the adaptational process." "The basis for the constructive effect of adaptation lies in three phenomena (Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, Viru, Kirge, 35, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286):
- specificity of protein synthesis in the after work period, conditioned by the character of the work executed, its intensity and means of energy provision,
- supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins),
- a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the muscular work."

From these he names "two levels of the constructive effect." "One of them is related to the well known phase of restitution that is inherent in the phenomenon of supercompensation of products and energy used up in external work (Yakovlev, 139, 144, Viru, 289). The other level is related to the long stages of training. It is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect (Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283)" (PDF 530 / p.519).

**Why it works** — The short level rests on restitution: the phase after work "is characterized not only by increased metabolism but also a higher turnover speed of the muscle proteins which ensures the renewal of the molecular composition of the actin - myosin complex," clearing "'physiologically exhausted' structural 'footprints'" (Viru, 289, 291). "The program of biochemical changes ... determine the catabolic processes taking place in the muscles during the time of work. This program is realized during the time of rest" (PDF 530 / p.519). Inference: the long level is the same process summed over a concentrated block; the page says only that it "is related to the long stages of training" (see [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]).

**When to apply** — Inference: use the two levels to keep two time scales apart when judging a plan. A session or microcycle is judged by restitution over hours to days; a concentrated block is judged by the delayed rise weeks after the loading, not by how the athlete performs during it.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the book contradicts itself on the second phenomenon. Here supercompensation covers "different structural and enzymatic proteins." In 1.16 the authors prefer "adaptive reconstruction," and the 1.16 text states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" (PDF 99 / p.88; see [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]). Same claim, same book. The page shows no data for either level. The link between the two levels (that the long-term effect is built from session-level restitution) is not stated on the page.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own definition of the long level: "the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads" (PDF 530 / p.519), the pattern drawn as strategy C in Fig 4 (see [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]]).

# Adaptation Is Heterochronic and Runs on Three Levels: Quick Homeostatic Reactions, Compensatory Structural Change, Long-Term Systemic Restructuring

**What it is** — 9.1 §1.6, "Heterochronism of the adaptational restructuring" (PDF 538 / p.527, checked against the page image). Verkhoshansky: "Development of the adaptation process is tied in with a definite heterochronicity in the formation of accommodative body restructuring. Heterochronicity appears first in the failure to coincide moments of time with the corresponding beginnings of the intense improvement of one or another functional system. Second, it appears in the specific consecutiveness of the adaptation reactions and development of morphofunctional restructuring of the body." The three levels, each with "its own specific character in regard to heterochronicity" (PDF 538-539 / pp.527-528):
1. "level of biochemical processes ensuring energy and plastic functions at the time of work and immediately after its conclusion (level of quick homeostatic reactions)";
2. "level of compensatory accommodation restructuring, in the foundation of which, are the structural (morphological) transformations in the body (level of compensatory adaptation)";
3. "level of global functional-systemic restructuring (level of long term steady adaptation)."
The first level is detailed by Fig 9 and Table 2 ([[framework--yakovlev-work-and-recovery-biosynthesis-chain-fig-9]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]]); the second and third by Fig 10 ([[claim--function-leads-structure-and-power-precedes-capacity-and-economy-fig-10]]).

**Why it works** — The stated causes of heterochronicity: "the changes in the external interactions of the body, a gradual increase in the intensity of the body work regime with an increase in sports mastery and with changes tied in with these roles in the maintenance of separate functional systems, and likewise with a definite inertness of different body systems (Verkhoshansky, 13, 17, Yakovlev, 144)" (PDF 538 / p.527).

**When to apply** — When reading a monitoring trend: a fast marker (a session's metabolic response) and a slow one (structural or whole-system change) are expected to move at different times, so a lack of change in a slow marker after a few weeks is not by itself a failed block. Inference: the three levels map onto session, block and multi-year time scales; the page names the levels but gives no durations for them.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a conceptual scheme with citations (Verkhoshansky 24, 25; Verkhoshansky and Viru 28, 286) and no data. The same three levels reappear in 1.10 on PDF 554 / p.543 (outside this batch); 9a's Viru scheme ([[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]]) is a related but separate sequence (specific, general, long-term). The page says more on heterochronicity is in "the section on laws of morphofunctional specialization" (PDF 540 / p.529), which is outside this batch.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own level 1: "fast flowing biochemical processes activated in a definite consecutiveness during work and post work periods (Figure 9)" (PDF 539 / p.528).

# The Current Adaptation Reserve Has a Ceiling Set by Two Factors, and It Shrinks as an Athlete Nears the Genetic Limit

**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.2, "Current adaptation reserves of the body," Verkhoshansky describes the compensatory phase as one of "intense mobilization of the energy and plastic reserves of the body. This phase cannot be long." After it, "the body recovers its functions up to a level which significantly surpasses the initial" (9.1 §1.2, PDF 521 / p.510, checked against the page image). "This is the beginning hypothesis of the current adaptation reserve (CAR), which the body always has available for extreme situations that may arise requiring maximum functional loading (Verkhoshansky, 1985- 24, 1988 - 282, 1993 - 27)." Two new points follow. First, "The volume of CAR has a definite limit, which is conditional (as determined from specialized studies) based on two factors: the adaptation (functional) reserve of the sympathetic-adrenal and hypophysial - adrenocorticoid systems (Viru, 

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's mechanism: the first factor is hormonal, the same two systems that fund energy and plastic mobilisation under stress (see [[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]]). The second is how much restructuring has already happened. Inference: the more an athlete has already adapted, the less distance is left to the genetic limit, so each block can buy less.

**When to apply** — Inference: when an advanced athlete's gains from a block are smaller than a younger athlete's from the same block, this account says that is expected, not a programming failure. It also argues for spending the reserve with care in elite athletes, since there is less of it.

**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky calls CAR a "hypothesis" ("the beginning hypothesis") and the "specialized studies" that set its two limits are not shown; no measure of CAR is given, so it cannot be tested or tracked from this page. The genetic-limit reading rests on his own books (refs 24, 27, 282). Rated `untested`; the existing 6.8.1 entry on dosing within CAR is rated `supported` on the authors' fuller Chapter 6 account.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own evidence that a reserve exists is indirect: "the presence of the adaptation reserve in the body is seen in cases of accidents (wrecks)" (Yakovlev, Prokop, Beckman, Letunov, Garkavi; PDF 522 / p.511). He gives no sport example on these pages.

# Load Must Sit Inside the Current Adaptation Reserve Window: Too Little Wastes It, Too Much Exhausts It

**What it is** — The authors make the current adaptation reserves (CAR) a programming rule (PDF p. 359 / printed p. 348, checked against the page image): "At any instant, the body has a definite reserve potential, i.e. a capability of responding to adapt to external influences and raise itself to a new functional level," limited by "definite physiological mechanisms." Hence "the intensity, volume and duration of the training influences determine the optimal development of the body's CAR. If the magnitude of these are below certain thresholds, the body will not fully utilise its CAR, whereas, if they exceed it, exhaustion of reserve potential will occur and the training effect will be low or negative."

The goal follows: "one can consider training organisation to be effective when it produces the maximum growth of the body's CAR by means of the appropriate volume of loading." Useful programming therefore needs "means of assessing the body's CAR in each case, together with criteria for determining the contents and volume of the training loads," and a quantitative approach "is based, in particular, on assessments of a number of bio-chemical indicators of energy exchange processes (Beckman et al, 1961; Yakovlev, 1977)" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349, checked against the page image).

The authors place this inside the older three-phase schemes of form: "(a) the growth of trainability, (b) sporting form, (c) loss of trainability (Letunov, 1952)"; "(a) adaptation, (b) the highest sport work-capacity, (c) re-adaptation (Prokor, 1959)," where re-adaptation is "decrease in work capacity as the limits of adaptability are exceeded" (PDF pp. 359-360 / printed pp. 348-349); and Matveyev's "acquisition, preservation and brief loss of sporting form (Matveyev, 1964)" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349). "Prokor" is the book's spelling.

**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is a threshold model: a reserve with a fixed size at any moment is under-used by small loads and depleted by large ones. They give no measured threshold. Inference: Bompa's threshold-of-adaptation entry (Related) sets out three outcomes of loading (an increasing, varied load, adaptation; an unchanging load, plateau; an excessive one, maladaptation) at the level of single loads; the authors apply it to a whole training phase.

**When to apply** — Inference: when a block produces no gain, ask first whether the load was below threshold (too little) or beyond it (exhaustion); the remedy is opposite in the two cases. The authors' wave signal (see Related) is one way to tell: waves in special work capacity mark the reserve running out. Eric's baseline: the mRSI decision read uses individualized thresholds, "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). Inference: that is a practical, non-biochemical stand-in for the "means of assessing the body's CAR" the authors ask for, read at the weekly scale.

**When NOT to apply** — The page names biochemical indicators only in general and cites 1961 and 1977 work; no assay, threshold or validated CAR measure is given. Chapter 1 gives two conflicting definitions of CAR (the readily available energy versus the deep adaptation energy; see [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]); this section does not settle which is meant. Inference: treat CAR as a planning concept, not a measurable quantity.

**Example** — The authors' own application follows on the same page: the durations of continuous and concentrated loading blocks that they say maximally enhance the CAR (see [[heuristic--concentrated-blocks-of-3-4-weeks-three-in-a-row-then-longer-recovery]]).

**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[claim--compensatory-adaptation-is-temporary-and-precedes-stable-adaptation]], [[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]], [[heuristic--concentrated-blocks-of-3-4-weeks-three-in-a-row-then-longer-recovery]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--verkhoshansky-activation-levels-and-threshold-of-adaptability]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]], [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]] (6.9.4, volume as the "disturbance of the body's homeostasis"). From 9.1: [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]] (9.1, what sets the size of CAR).

**Also in 9.1** — Verkhoshansky restates the rule in 9.1 §1.2 (PDF 522 / p.511, checked against the page image): "If the strength (magnitude), volume and duration of the training influences are below the necessary (optimal) amounts, CAR will not be realized; if they go above it, it leads to extreme exhaustion of the reserve capabilities. In both cases, the resulting training effect will be low (Verkhoshansky,Viru, 28, 286)." New in 9.1 are the two factors that cap CAR and its shrinkage with mastery: see [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]].

61	- supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins),
62	- a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the muscular work."
63	
64	From these he names "two levels of the constructive effect." "One of them is related to the well known phase of restitution that is inherent in the phenomenon of supercompensation of products and energy used up in external work (Yakovlev, 139, 144, Viru, 289). The other level is related to the long stages of training. It is expressed in the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads, is known as the long term delayed training effect (Verkhoshansky, 23, 24, 25, 280, 281, 282, 283)" (PDF 530 / p.519).
65	
66	**Why it works** — The short level rests on restitution: the phase after work "is characterized not only by increased metabolism but also a higher turnover speed of the muscle proteins which ensures the renewal of the molecular composition of the actin - myosin complex," clearing "'physiologically exhausted' structural 'footprints'" (Viru, 289, 291). "The program of biochemical changes ... determine the catabolic processes taking place in the muscles during the time of work. This program is realized during the time of rest" (PDF 530 / p.519). Inference: the long level is the same process summed over a concentrated block; the page says only that it "is related to the long stages of training" (see [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]).
67	
68	**When to apply** — Inference: use the two levels to keep two time scales apart when judging a plan. A session or microcycle is judged by restitution over hours to days; a concentrated block is judged by the delayed rise weeks after the loading, not by how the athlete performs during it.
69	
70	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `contested` because the book contradicts itself on the second phenomenon. Here supercompensation covers "different structural and enzymatic proteins." In 1.16 the authors prefer "adaptive reconstruction," and the 1.16 text states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" (PDF 99 / p.88; see [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]). Same claim, same book. The page shows no data for either level. The link between the two levels (that the long-term effect is built from session-level restitution) is not stated on the page.
71	
72	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own definition of the long level: "the long and steady increase in the functional indices after their long decrease as a result of using concentrated training loads" (PDF 530 / p.519), the pattern drawn as strategy C in Fig 4 (see [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]]).
73	
74	**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]] (6.10), [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]] (4.1.2, the authors' names for effects on different time scales). From the next pages of 9.1: [[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]] (the short level, Fig 6), [[claim--restitution-scales-with-work-expenditure-and-sets-adaptive-biosynthesis]] (the third basis spelled out, PDF 535 / p.524), [[claim--supercompensation-laws-extend-to-concentrated-spp-stages-of-10-12-weeks]] (PDF 535 / p.524 states that the supercompensation laws also apply to concentrated SPP stages of 10-1

82	# Adaptation Is Heterochronic and Runs on Three Levels: Quick Homeostatic Reactions, Compensatory Structural Change, Long-Term Systemic Restructuring
83	
84	**What it is** — 9.1 §1.6, "Heterochronism of the adaptational restructuring" (PDF 538 / p.527, checked against the page image). Verkhoshansky: "Development of the adaptation process is tied in with a definite heterochronicity in the formation of accommodative body restructuring. Heterochronicity appears first in the failure to coincide moments of time with the corresponding beginnings of the intense improvement of one or another functional system. Second, it appears in the specific consecutiveness of the adaptation reactions and development of morphofunctional restructuring of the body." The three levels, each with "its own specific character in regard to heterochronicity" (PDF 538-539 / pp.527-528):
85	1. "level of biochemical processes ensuring energy and plastic functions at the time of work and immediately after its conclusion (level of quick homeostatic reactions)";
86	2. "level of compensatory accommodation restructuring, in the foundation of which, are the structural (morphological) transformations in the body (level of compensatory adaptation)";
87	3. "level of global functional-systemic restructuring (level of long term steady adaptation)."
88	The first level is detailed by Fig 9 and Table 2 ([[framework--yakovlev-work-and-recovery-biosynthesis-chain-fig-9]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]]); the second and third by Fig 10 ([[claim--function-leads-structure-and-power-precedes-capacity-and-economy-fig-10]]).
89	
90	**Why it works** — The stated causes of heterochronicity: "the changes in the external interactions of the body, a gradual increase in the intensity of the body work regime with an increase in sports mastery and with changes tied in with these roles in the maintenance of separate functional systems, and likewise with a definite inertness of different body systems (Verkhoshansky, 13, 17, Yakovlev, 144)" (PDF 538 / p.527).
91	
92	**When to apply** — When reading a monitoring trend: a fast marker (a session's metabolic response) and a slow one (structural or whole-system change) are expected to move at different times, so a lack of change in a slow marker after a few weeks is not by itself a failed block. Inference: the three levels map onto session, block and multi-year time scales; the page names the levels but gives no durations for them.
93	
94	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a conceptual scheme with citations (Verkhoshansky 24, 25; Verkhoshansky and Viru 28, 286) and no data. The same three levels reappear in 1.10 on PDF 554 / p.543 (outside this batch); 9a's Viru scheme ([[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]]) is a related but separate sequence (specific, general, long-term). The page says more on heterochronicity is in "the section on laws of morphofunctional specialization" (PDF 540 / p.529), which is outside this batch.
95	
96	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own level 1: "fast flowing biochemical processes activated in a definite consecutiveness during work and post work periods (Figure 9)" (PDF 539 / p.528).

106	# The Current Adaptation Reserve Has a Ceiling Set by Two Factors, and It Shrinks as an Athlete Nears the Genetic Limit
107	
108	**What it is** — In 9.1 section 1.2, "Current adaptation reserves of the body," Verkhoshansky describes the compensatory phase as one of "intense mobilization of the energy and plastic reserves of the body. This phase cannot be long." After it, "the body recovers its functions up to a level which significantly surpasses the initial" (9.1 §1.2, PDF 521 / p.510, checked against the page image). "This is the beginning hypothesis of the current adaptation reserve (CAR), which the body always has available for extreme situations that may arise requiring maximum functional loading (Verkhoshansky, 1985- 24, 1988 - 282, 1993 - 27)." Two new points follow. First, "The volume of CAR has a definite limit, which is conditional (as determined from specialized studies) based on two factors: the adaptation (functional) reserve of the sympathetic-adrenal and hypophysial - adrenocorticoid systems (Viru, 
109	
110	**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's mechanism: the first factor is hormonal, the same two systems that fund energy and plastic mobilisation under stress (see [[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]]). The second is how much restructuring has already happened. Inference: the more an athlete has already adapted, the less distance is left to the genetic limit, so each block can buy less.
111	
112	**When to apply** — Inference: when an advanced athlete's gains from a block are smaller than a younger athlete's from the same block, this account says that is expected, not a programming failure. It also argues for spending the reserve with care in elite athletes, since there is less of it.
113	
114	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky calls CAR a "hypothesis" ("the beginning hypothesis") and the "specialized studies" that set its two limits are not shown; no measure of CAR is given, so it cannot be tested or tracked from this page. The genetic-limit reading rests on his own books (refs 24, 27, 282). Rated `untested`; the existing 6.8.1 entry on dosing within CAR is rated `supported` on the authors' fuller Chapter 6 account.
115	
116	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own evidence that a reserve exists is indirect: "the presence of the adaptation reserve in the body is seen in cases of accidents (wrecks)" (Yakovlev, Prokop, Beckman, Letunov, Garkavi; PDF 522 / p.511). He gives no sport example on these pages.
117	
118	**Related** — [[principle--load-must-sit-within-the-current-adaptation-reserve-window]] (6.8.1, the dosing rule), [[heuristic--concentrated-blocks-of-3-4-weeks-three-in-a-row-then-longer-recovery]] (how long it takes to exhaust CAR), [[claim--speed-barrier-is-genetic-ceiling-not-neural-block]] (another genetic-ceiling argument in the book), [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[framework--three-adaptation-strategies-low-uniform-high-and-concentrated-fig-4]]

120	kind: principle
121	chapter: "6.8.1"
122	topic: current adaptation reserves
123	category: [adaptation, training-load, overtraining, programming]
124	confidence: supported
125	
126	# Load Must Sit Inside the Current Adaptation Reserve Window: Too Little Wastes It, Too Much Exhausts It
127	
128	**What it is** — The authors make the current adaptation reserves (CAR) a programming rule (PDF p. 359 / printed p. 348, checked against the page image): "At any instant, the body has a definite reserve potential, i.e. a capability of responding to adapt to external influences and raise itself to a new functional level," limited by "definite physiological mechanisms." Hence "the intensity, volume and duration of the training influences determine the optimal development of the body's CAR. If the magnitude of these are below certain thresholds, the body will not fully utilise its CAR, whereas, if they exceed it, exhaustion of reserve potential will occur and the training effect will be low or negative."
129	
130	The goal follows: "one can consider training organisation to be effective when it produces the maximum growth of the body's CAR by means of the appropriate volume of loading." Useful programming therefore needs "means of assessing the body's CAR in each case, together with criteria for determining the contents and volume of the training loads," and a quantitative approach "is based, in particular, on assessments of a number of bio-chemical indicators of energy exchange processes (Beckman et al, 1961; Yakovlev, 1977)" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349, checked against the page image).
131	
132	The authors place this inside the older three-phase schemes of form: "(a) the growth of trainability, (b) sporting form, (c) loss of trainability (Letunov, 1952)"; "(a) adaptation, (b) the highest sport work-capacity, (c) re-adaptation (Prokor, 1959)," where re-adaptation is "decrease in work capacity as the limits of adaptability are exceeded" (PDF pp. 359-360 / printed pp. 348-349); and Matveyev's "acquisition, preservation and brief loss of sporting form (Matveyev, 1964)" (PDF p. 360 / printed p. 349). "Prokor" is the book's spelling.
133	
134	**Why it works** — The authors' reasoning is a threshold model: a reserve with a fixed size at any moment is under-used by small loads and depleted by large ones. They give no measured threshold. Inference: Bompa's threshold-of-adaptation entry (Related) sets out three outcomes of loading (an increasing, varied load, adaptation; an unchanging load, plateau; an excessive one, maladaptation) at the level of single loads; the authors apply it to a whole training phase.
135	
136	**When to apply** — Inference: when a block produces no gain, ask first whether the load was below threshold (too little) or beyond it (exhaustion); the remedy is opposite in the two cases. The authors' wave signal (see Related) is one way to tell: waves in special work capacity mark the reserve running out. Eric's baseline: the mRSI decision read uses individualized thresholds, "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). Inference: that is a practical, non-biochemical stand-in for the "means of assessing the body's CAR" the authors ask for, read at the weekly scale.
137	
138	**When NOT to apply** — The page names biochemical indicators only in general and cites 1961 and 1977 work; no assay, threshold or validated CAR measure is given. Chapter 1 gives two conflicting definitions of CAR (the readily available energy versus the deep adaptation energy; see [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]); this section does not settle which is meant. Inference: treat CAR as a planning concept, not a measurable quantity.
139	
140	**Example** — The authors' own application follows on the same page: the durations of continuous and concentrated loading blocks that they say maximally enhance the CAR (see [[heuristic--concentrated-blocks-of-3-4-weeks-three-in-a-row-then-longer-recovery]]).
141	
142	**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[claim--compensatory-adaptation-is-temporary-and-precedes-stable-adaptation]], [[framework--distributed-vs-concentrated-loading-two-forms-of-compensatory-adaptation]], [[heuristic--concentrated-blocks-of-3-4-weeks-three-in-a-row-then-longer-recovery]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--verkhoshansky-activation-levels-and-threshold-of-adaptability]], [[periodization--bompa/principle--progressive-overload-threshold]], [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]] (6.9.4, volume as the "disturbance of the body's homeostasis"). From 9.1: [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]] (9.1, what sets the size of CAR).
143	
144	**Also in 9.1** — Verkhoshansky restates the rule in 9.1 §1.2 (PDF 522 / p.511, checked against the page image): "If the strength (magnitude), volume and duration of the training influences are below the necessary (optimal) amounts, CAR will not be realized; if they go above it, it leads to extreme exhaustion of the reserve capabilities. In both cases, the resulting training effect will be low (Verkhoshansky,Viru, 28, 286)." New in 9.1 are the two factors that cap CAR and its shrinkage with mastery: see [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]].

149	category: [training-theory, long-term-development, programming]
150	confidence: untested
151	
152	# Training Theory as a Hierarchy: Laws of Adaptation, Then Laws of Sports Mastery, Then Principles, Then the Time Forms of Training (Fig 3)
153	
154	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky opens 9.1 with the "multi year Process of Achieving Sports Mastery (PASM)," which "was developed on a base of definite laws. Athletes can achieve the heights of sports mastery by different pathways and expend different amounts of time doing this. However, the path taken by each athlete will have general traits, inherent to all athletes," set by "genetically imposed abilities of the body to accommodate" (9.1 Introduction, PDF 515 / p.504, checked against the page image). "The general laws of PASM are first of all determined by the laws of development of the adaptational process related to sports activity (Figure 3)" (PDF 519 / p.508). Figure 3 ("The principal structure of the fundamentals of the Theory and Methodology of Sport Training," PDF 520 / p.509, read from the image; no source is given) stacks: "The laws of adaptation"; "General laws of PASM"; two br
155	
156	**Why it works** — His argument: "The general laws of the PASM reflect the necessary structure of multiyear training in an objective manner, including the order of development of all of its components and the principles of their interactions." The principles are "joined with the objective display of the practical realization of the laws of adaptation of the body to loaded muscular activity, to determine the organizational-temporal form of constructing sports training" (PDF 520 / p.509). Other drivers of mastery, "socio-economic conditions, effectiveness of the theoretical concept of training, professional mastery of the coach, the individual psycho-physiological personality traits of the athlete and so on," are, "even with the indubitable significance of these factors, ... secondary. They can be looked at (and realized) under the process of PASM, but do not determine the principle mechan
157	
158	**When to apply** — As an order of questions when building or auditing a plan: what adaptation is wanted, what the sport's specialisation and technical demands require, which principles follow, and only then how to lay out years, blocks, weeks, days and sessions. Inference: the figure puts the calendar last, which is the reverse of building a plan by filling a template of weeks.
159	
160	**When NOT to apply** — Verkhoshansky states that "It has been proven that the unique correct path to the formulation of effective practical principles of sports training is through the clarification of the laws of human body adaptation" (PDF 519 / p.508), but the page cites his own and colleagues' work, not a test of that claim; it is his position, rated `untested` here. The figure has no source line and no data. Inference: for a team-sport staff, the factors he calls "secondary" (coach skill, the athlete's personality, budgets and schedules) often set the real limits, so the hierarchy describes the logic of a plan, not what most constrains it.
161	
162	**Example** — Fig 3 (PDF 520 / p.509): the five time forms at the bottom, from "Yearly cycle" down to the single "Training seance," all hang from "The forms of the temporal organization of training," which hangs from the principles and, above them, the laws of adaptation.
163
