# Study Adaptation as a Process: Track the Athlete's State Over Long Stages Against the Loads Actually Done, and Look for the Mechanism, Not Only the Outcome

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 Further perspectives, PDF 560-561 / pp.549-550, checked against the page images): "The theory of adaptation plays its methodological and scientific-practical role in the theory and methods and sports training only in those cases if attention to it is concentrated not on the phenomena (external side), but on its physiological mechanism." Studies of "not only, and not so much, the external side of the adaptation process" are needed, chiefly those on "the hormonal mechanisms of the non-specific component of long term adaptation" (Meerson and Pshennikova, 78; Viru, 32, 291). "However, an especially important applied value that will be gotten from investigations oriented to the study of not only the results, but the process of long term adaptation to sports activity, its concrete quantitative-temporal parameters ... and frequently the laws of morphofunctional specialization of the athlete's body in the process of multi-year training ... and tendencies in the dynamic state of the athletes in the yearly cycle under the influence of the given training loads" (PDF 560 / p.549; citations cut). On the next page, after Yakovlev's three tasks, he adds: "the practical methods of experimentally studying the problems of adaptation should be based mainly on the study of the tendencies (laws) in the dynamics of the athletes state during long term stages of preparation in relation to the training loads executed (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, Verkhoshansky et al. 22, 279)" (PDF 561 / p.550).

**Why it works** — A result shows that something changed; the time course of state against load shows when and why, which is what a plan needs to repeat or correct it. Inference: pairing load with state over a whole stage is what lets delayed effects (such as the long-term delayed training effect) be seen at all.

**When to apply** — Keep a running record of the loads actually done, not only those planned, alongside repeated state measures across the whole block and year, and read them together. Eric's review: the department reads mRSI against "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). Inference: that is a state-dynamics series in Verkhoshansky's sense; his point adds that it should be read against executed load across a long stage, not only week to week.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a research agenda, not a tested method; it names no measures, sampling rate or analysis. The stress on hormonal mechanisms reflects the Soviet adaptation school he cites. Inference: for a staff without lab access, the "mechanism" half of the advice is often out of reach, and the state-versus-load series is the usable part.

**Example** — His own named target: "tendencies in the dynamic state of the athletes in the yearly cycle under the influence of the given training loads (Verkhosh­ansky et al 22, 279)" (PDF 560 / p.549).

**Related** — [[principle--training-theory-must-rest-on-adaptation-and-be-written-by-physiological-state-dynamics]], [[framework--logical-scheme-of-training-management-load-fitness-state-external-interactions]] (6.4), [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[framework--yakovlev-three-applied-tasks-of-sports-biochemistry]], [[principle--pair-objective-and-subjective-tests-because-rpe-can-miss-a-poor-functional-state]]

# Study Adaptation as a Process: Track the Athlete's State Over Long Stages Against the Loads Actually Done, and Look for the Mechanism, Not Only the Outcome

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 Further perspectives, PDF 560-561 / pp.549-550, checked against the page images): "The theory of adaptation plays its methodological and scientific-practical role in the theory and methods and sports training only in those cases if attention to it is concentrated not on the phenomena (external side), but on its physiological mechanism." Studies of "not only, and not so much, the external side of the adaptation process" are needed, chiefly those on "the hormonal mechanisms of the non-specific component of long term adaptation" (Meerson and Pshennikova, 78; Viru, 32, 291). "However, an especially important applied value that will be gotten from investigations oriented to the study of not only the results, but the process of long term adaptation to sports activity, its concrete quantitative-temporal parameters ... and frequently the laws of morphofunctional specialization of the athlete's body in the process of multi-year training ... and tendencies in the dynamic state of the athletes in the yearly cycle under the influence of the given training loads" (PDF 560 / p.549; citations cut). On the next page, after Yakovlev's three tasks, he adds: "the practical methods of experimentally studying the problems of adaptation should be based mainly on the study of the tendencies (laws) in the dynamics of the athletes state during long term stages of preparation in relation to the training loads executed (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, Verkhoshansky et al. 22, 279)" (PDF 561 / p.550).

**Why it works** — A result shows that something changed; the time course of state against load shows when and why, which is what a plan needs to repeat or correct it. Inference: pairing load with state over a whole stage is what lets delayed effects (such as the long-term delayed training effect) be seen at all.

**When to apply** — Keep a running record of the loads actually done, not only those planned, alongside repeated state measures across the whole block and year, and read them together. Eric's review: the department reads mRSI against "Percent change from baseline or a rolling average. We've used standard deviations and SWC to diagnose signal versus noise" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 75, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q2, Q2a)). Inference: that is a state-dynamics series in Verkhoshansky's sense; his point adds that it should be read against executed load across a long stage, not only week to week.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a research agenda, not a tested method; it names no measures, sampling rate or analysis. The stress on hormonal mechanisms reflects the Soviet adaptation school he cites. Inference: for a staff without lab access, the "mechanism" half of the advice is often out of reach, and the state-versus-load series is the usable part.

**Example** — His own named target: "tendencies in the dynamic state of the athletes in the yearly cycle under the influence of the given training loads (Verkhosh­ansky et al 22, 279)" (PDF 560 / p.549).

**Related** — [[principle--training-theory-must-rest-on-adaptation-and-be-written-by-physiological-state-dynamics]], [[framework--logical-scheme-of-training-management-load-fitness-state-external-interactions]] (6.4), [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[framework--yakovlev-three-applied-tasks-of-sports-biochemistry]], [[principle--pair-objective-and-subjective-tests-because-rpe-can-miss-a-poor-functional-state]]

# Yakovlev's Three Applied Tasks for Sports Biochemistry: Intensify Adaptation in the Trained Body, Speed Restitution, Find Tests of Trainedness

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky reports N.N. Yakovlev's agenda (9.1 Further perspectives, PDF 561 / p.550, checked against the page image), noting it was "concretely formed by N.N. Yakovlev even 40 years ago" and set out in three articles (1971, 1972, 1976). "According to Yakovlev, practical tasks in the biochemistry of sport, orientated to the study of applied problems of adaptation of man to loaded (sports) muscle activity, can be formulated into three points:
1. Finding ways of increasing the intensity of the adaptational changes in the highly trained body;
2. Finding ways of speeding up biochemical restitution;
3. Finding biochemical tests to evaluate trainedness in speed-strength and technical type sports."

The paragraphs that follow give a route for each. Task 1: find "supplementary factors that bring about disturbance of the homeostasis similar to those that are observed during muscular activity" (see Related). Task 2: "speeding up restoration, should go along the pathway of further effective nutrition for the athletes and the use of physical factors: massage, hydro procedures and physiotherapy." Task 3: "The third task is the most difficult. What can help to some extent is the study of the ATP balance in the working muscles." The page does not mark where Yakovlev's account ends and Verkhoshansky's begins; the three route paragraphs read as continued exposition of Yakovlev, and the sentence that follows ("For this it follows to add that ...", citing Verkhoshansky's own refs) is Verkhoshansky's addition.

**Why it works** — Task 1 rests on the trained body's smaller homeostatic disturbance (the same work leaves less behind to drive adaptation); task 2 on restitution being where synthesis happens; task 3 on the lack of good markers for non-endurance sports.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a checklist when choosing support work for advanced athletes: what raises the adaptive signal without more training load, what speeds recovery when recovery is the aim, and what marker tells you trainedness in a power or technical sport.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: an agenda from the 1970s, with no data on the page. Task 2 sits in tension with Verkhoshansky's own §1.5, where procedures that speed metabolite removal "leads to a disturbance in protein synthesis and as a result, to a decrease in training effect" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). This entry reads the task 2 route as Yakovlev's position reported by Verkhoshansky, not as Verkhoshansky's own claim, so it is a difference between a cited author and the paper's author, not a self-contradiction, and is not marked `contested`. Inference: the two can be reconciled by timing (speed restoration when the next session matters more than the last one's signal), but the page does not say so.

**Example** — Yakovlev's task 3 and its partial answer: tests "to evaluate trainedness in speed-strength and technical type sports," helped "to some extent" by "the study of the ATP balance in the working muscles" (PDF 561 / p.550).

**Related** — [[claim--when-loads-cannot-rise-further-add-supplementary-homeostasis-disturbing-factors]] (task 1), [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (6.9.3), [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]], [[framework--yakovlev-work-and-recovery-biosynthesis-chain-fig-9]], [[heuristic--study-the-adaptation-process-by-tracking-state-dynamics-against-executed-loads]]

# When Training Load Can No Longer Rise Without Harm, Seek Supplementary Factors That Disturb Homeostasis the Way Muscular Work Does

**What it is** — The route given for Yakovlev's first task, "Finding ways of increasing the intensity of the adaptational changes in the highly trained body" (9.1 Further perspectives, PDF 561 / p.550, checked against the page image): "In resolving the first task, it appears to be rational to proceed from the level of disturbance of the biochemical homeostasis during execution of the training loads. With an increase in trainedness this disturbance decreases, and the less it becomes, the less are the following consequences remaining from the muscular activity and that lie in the base of adaptation. Because of this, with an increase in trainedness, it becomes inevitable that the training loads should increase. However, on the contemporary stage of sports development we cannot practically further increase the intensity and duration of the training loads without harming the body. A more realistic path here is to find supplementary factors that bring about disturbance of the homeostasis similar to those that are observed during muscular activity. As a result, this means strengthening the following consequent appearances, left by the latter."

**Why it works** — The first half restates 9.1 §1.5: a trained body is disturbed less by the same work, so less is left to drive adaptation (see Related). The new step is the ceiling: if load cannot rise further without harm, the extra disturbance has to come from outside the training load and add to the after-effects the training leaves.

**When to apply** — Inference: for an athlete whose volume and intensity are already at the limit, look for added stressors that act on the same systems rather than more of the same work. The page names none; candidates a reader might consider (altitude or hypoxia, heat) are the writer's examples, not the book's.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a reasoned proposal with no data and no named factor. Attribution: the paragraph follows Yakovlev's list and reads as continued exposition of his position; the page does not mark it as Verkhoshansky's own. The "contemporary stage" is the late 1980s to early 1990s elite Soviet system; the claim that loads cannot rise further is about athletes at that ceiling, not about developing athletes, whose loads can still rise. Inference: an added stressor also adds to total stress, so it competes with recovery and with the CAR limits set out earlier in 9.1.

**Example** — The two steps in his own words: "with an increase in trainedness, it becomes inevitable that the training loads should increase," then "we cannot practically further increase the intensity and duration of the training loads without harming the body" (PDF 561 / p.550).

**Related** — [[claim--trainedness-is-the-sum-of-session-after-effects-and-lowers-homeostatic-disturbance]] (§1.5, the smaller disturbance in a trained body), [[framework--yakovlev-three-applied-tasks-of-sports-biochemistry]], [[claim--car-volume-is-capped-and-shrinks-as-mastery-nears-the-genetic-limit]], [[claim--automatic-defence-reserve-of-about-30-percent-of-car-is-off-limits-in-natural-training]], [[claim--ldte-in-endurance-training-documented-only-after-altitude-training]]

# Directing Adaptation in Future: Unite Optimal Loading Regimes, Non-Specific Methods of Raising Workability, and Selection of the Most Adaptable People

**What it is** — The closing page of 9.1 (Further perspectives, PDF 561-562 / pp.550-551, checked against the page images). Verkhoshansky expects that "attention of investigators will be re-oriented toward more simple registration of the dynamics of the functional state in the process of accommodation of the body to the surroundings and activity directing adaptation (Meerson, 76, 77, Medvedev, 73)." "Such directing, apparently, will become possible as a result of uniting:
1) the optimal regimes of influencing the adaptive factor,
2) non-specific methods of increasing physical workability
3) the selection of people, most adaptable to the influence of the adaptive factor."
"The aim of such a complex approach will speed up the accommodative process, decrease its physiological and psychological cost, lengthen the period during which the state of adaptation is maintained, and increase the economic effectiveness of the methods of adaptation used (Medvedev, 73, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 286)." The paper ends: "Today it is necessary to have scientific erudition and experimental-theoretical unification to seriously resolve this problem" (PDF 562 / p.551).

**Why it works** — Each part acts on a different lever: the right dose (regime), help from outside the training load (non-specific methods), and starting with people who respond well (selection). Together they aim at four outcomes: faster adaptation, lower cost, longer retention, better economy of means.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a frame for reviewing a support programme: is the loading regime set to the adaptation wanted, what non-specific means (recovery, nutrition, other stressors) are used, and does selection take responsiveness into account. The four aims give the review its yardsticks.

# When Training Load Can No Longer Rise Without Harm, Seek Supplementary Factors That Disturb Homeostasis the Way Muscular Work Does

**What it is** — The route given for Yakovlev's first task, "Finding ways of increasing the intensity of the adaptational changes in the highly trained body" (9.1 Further perspectives, PDF 561 / p.550, checked against the page image): "In resolving the first task, it appears to be rational to proceed from the level of disturbance of the biochemical homeostasis during execution of the training loads. With an increase in trainedness this disturbance decreases, and the less it becomes, the less are the following consequences remaining from the muscular activity and that lie in the base of adaptation. Because of this, with an increase in trainedness, it becomes inevitable that the training loads should increase. However, on the contemporary stage of sports development we cannot practically further increase the intensity and duration of the training loads without harming the body. A more realistic path here is to find supplementary factors that bring about disturbance of the homeostasis similar to those that are observed during muscular activity. As a result, this means strengthening the following consequent appearances, left by the latter."

**Why it works** — The first half restates 9.1 §1.5: a trained body is disturbed less by the same work, so less is left to drive adaptation (see Related). The new step is the ceiling: if load cannot rise further without harm, the extra disturbance has to come from outside the training load and add to the after-effects the training leaves.

**When to apply** — Inference: for an athlete whose volume and intensity are already at the limit, look for added stressors that act on the same systems rather than more of the same work. The page names none; candidates a reader might consider (altitude or hypoxia, heat) are the writer's examples, not the book's.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a reasoned proposal with no data and no named factor. Attribution: the paragraph follows Yakovlev's list and reads as continued exposition of his position; the page does not mark it as Verkhoshansky's own. The "contemporary stage" is the late 1980s to early 1990s elite Soviet system; the claim that loads cannot rise further is about athletes at that ceiling, not about developing athletes, whose loads can still rise. Inference: an added stressor also adds to total stress, so it competes with recovery and with the CAR limits set out earlier in 9.1.

**Example** — The two steps in his own words: "with an increase in trainedness, it becomes inevitable that the training loads should increase," then "we cannot practically further increase the intensity and duration of the training loads without harming the body" (PDF 561 / p.550).

# Long-Term Adaptation in Three Levels: Specific Homeostatic Reactions, Non-Specific Mechanisms, Then Stable Morpho-Functional Change (Fig 15)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.10, PDF 554-555 / pp.543-544, checked against the page images): "It is correct to propose that this process develops both vertically as well as horizontally (Verkhoshansky, Viru, 28, 286)," that is, "the accommodative restructurings have a concrete level of structure, functioning within the limits of definite segments (phases) of coordinated time (Figure 15)." The levels:
1. "The process of adaptation begins with activation of specific homeostatic reactions (first level of adaptation)."
2. "Repeat shifts in constant internal surroundings in the body and strengthening the reserves of energy and plastic provision brings about activation of non-specific mechanisms of adaptation and transition to compensatory adaptation (second level)."
3. "The mechanism of compensatory adaptation provides relatively stoic morpho-functional improvement in the cellular structure, which appears as an unchanging condition for development of long term adaptation, transforming the body into a new, higher level of specialized capabilities (third level)" (PDF 554 / p.543; "stoic" as printed).

He concludes that "compensatory adaptation is an intermediate link between short term and steady accommodative reactions," and that long-term adaptation "is a phasic multi-step accumulation process. It is developed on the multiple short term repetition mechanism of compensatory adaptation and periodic deductions in the fund of stabilized steady accommodative restructuring of morpho-functional 'surpluses', acquired by the body on the hemeostatic and non-specific reaction level" (PDF 555 / p.544; "hemeostatic" as printed).

Fig 15, "The structure of the process of long-term adaptation to the intensive muscular work" (PDF 554 / p.543, read from a 220 dpi render; no source given), is a staircase of four boxes: "Activation of specific homeostatic reactions," "Activation of nonspecific mechanism of adaptation," "Morphological-functional improvement of molecular structures," and at the top right "Specific work capacity." Solid arrows run up from each box to the next. Dashed lines run from each upper box back down to the box below it, and dashed lines also run from the two lower boxes across to the vertical line that rises into "Specific work capacity." Three brackets under the diagram appear to span, left to right: from the homeostatic box to the non-specific box, labelled "Compensatory adaptation"; from the non-specific box to the morpho-functional box, "General adaptation"; and from the morpho-functional box to the work-capacity line, "Realization of motor potential."

**Why it works** — His mechanism: repeated homeostatic shifts plus built-up energy and plastic reserves switch on the non-specific (general) mechanisms; their structural products are then banked as stable change, and each turn sets "an objectively necessary level for the following repeat activation of specific homeostatic reactions and for temporary redistribution of the plastic reserves of the body" (PDF 555 / p.544). Inference: the dashed downward lines in Fig 15 read as each new level resetting the one below it, but the caption does not define solid versus dashed lines, so that reading is the writer's.

**When to apply** — Inference: use the three levels to decide what a monitoring marker can show. A session marker sits at level 1; a block that keeps disturbing homeostasis aims at level 2; only change that holds after the block counts as level 3. "Specific work capacity" is the output the figure ties all three to, so the test of the scheme is the sport-specific measure, not the biochemical one.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`. He says "Studies in multiple sports (Viru, 32, Kassil et al. 61, Verkhoshansky, 20, 24, 25) substantiate the correctness of the theoretical positions" (PDF 555 / p.544), but no data are shown. The figure's labels do not line up cleanly with the text: the text calls level 2 "compensatory adaptation," while the leftmost bracket labelled "Compensatory adaptation" seems to span levels 1 to 2 and the middle bracket is "General adaptation." The bracket spans are read from the image and are the writer's best reading. This three-level scheme is related to, but not the same as, the three levels of heterochronism in §1.6 (biochemical, compensatory, global systemic; see Related).

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own sentence for the middle link: "compensatory adaptation is an intermediate link between short term and steady accommodative reactions" (PDF 555 / p.544).

**Related** — [[framework--heterochronism-and-three-levels-of-adaptation-restructuring]] (§1.6), [[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]] (the specific-to-general switch, Fig 2), [[claim--compensatory-adaptation-is-temporary-and-precedes-stable-adaptation]] (6.8.1), [[claim--acute-adaptation-runs-at-the-limit-and-long-term-adaptation-needs-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--sport-adaptation-is-a-periodic-factor-and-long-term-adaptation-cycles-car-exhaustion-and-restoration]]

# Yakovlev's Three Applied Tasks for Sports Biochemistry: Intensify Adaptation in the Trained Body, Speed Restitution, Find Tests of Trainedness

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky reports N.N. Yakovlev's agenda (9.1 Further perspectives, PDF 561 / p.550, checked against the page image), noting it was "concretely formed by N.N. Yakovlev even 40 years ago" and set out in three articles (1971, 1972, 1976). "According to Yakovlev, practical tasks in the biochemistry of sport, orientated to the study of applied problems of adaptation of man to loaded (sports) muscle activity, can be formulated into three points:
1. Finding ways of increasing the intensity of the adaptational changes in the highly trained body;
2. Finding ways of speeding up biochemical restitution;
3. Finding biochemical tests to evaluate trainedness in speed-strength and technical type sports."

The paragraphs that follow give a route for each. Task 1: find "supplementary factors that bring about disturbance of the homeostasis similar to those that are observed during muscular activity" (see Related). Task 2: "speeding up restoration, should go along the pathway of further effective nutrition for the athletes and the use of physical factors: massage, hydro procedures and physiotherapy." Task 3: "The third task is the most difficult. What can help to some extent is the study of the ATP balance in the working muscles." The page does not mark where Yakovlev's account ends and Verkhoshansky's begins; the three route paragraphs read as continued exposition of Yakovlev, and the sentence that follows ("For this it follows to add that ...", citing Verkhoshansky's own refs) is Verkhoshansky's addition.

**Why it works** — Task 1 rests on the trained body's smaller homeostatic disturbance (the same work leaves less behind to drive adaptation); task 2 on restitution being where synthesis happens; task 3 on the lack of good markers for non-endurance sports.

**When to apply** — Inference: as a checklist when choosing support work for advanced athletes: what raises the adaptive signal without more training load, what speeds recovery when recovery is the aim, and what marker tells you trainedness in a power or technical sport.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: an agenda from the 1970s, with no data on the page. Task 2 sits in tension with Verkhoshansky's own §1.5, where procedures that speed metabolite removal "leads to a disturbance in protein synthesis and as a result, to a decrease in training effect" (PDF 531 / p.520; see [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]). This entry reads the task 2 route as Yakovlev's position reported by Verkhoshansky, not as Verkhoshansky's own claim, so it is a difference between a cited author and the paper's author, not a self-contradiction, and is not marked `contested`. Inference: the two can be reconciled by timing (speed restoration when the next session matters more than the last one's signal), but the page does not say so.

**Example** — Yakovlev's task 3 and its partial answer: tests "to evaluate trainedness in speed-strength and technical type sports," helped "to some extent" by "the study of the ATP balance in the working muscles" (PDF 561 / p.550).

**Related** — [[claim--when-loads-cannot-rise-further-add-supplementary-homeostasis-disturbing-factors]] (task 1), [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[heuristic--routine-artificial-restoration-can-blunt-adaptation]] (6.9.3), [[heuristic--time-restoration-to-when-work-capacity-is-next-needed]], [[framework--yakovlev-work-and-recovery-biosynthesis-chain-fig-9]], [[heuristic--study-the-adaptation-process-by-tracking-state-dynamics-against-executed-loads]]

# Two Routes to Rebuild Training Theory on Adaptation: the Large Cycle (Compensatory Adaptation) and the Short Forms, Microcycle, Day and Training Seance (Short-Term Adaptation)

**What it is** — In the Conclusions, "Applied aspects of the problem," Verkhoshansky (9.1, PDF 555-556 / pp.544-545, checked against the page images): "Two ways have been determined to reorganize contemporary theory and methods of sports training based on the content and laws of development of adaptation of mans' body to loaded muscle activity."
- **First way.** "related to the principle of constructing the training and is directly tied in with the mechanism of compensatory adaptation and understanding the large (macro) training cycle." "The large training cycle is principally a new form of organizing the training process in the theory of sport. It is tied in with the aim of realizing CAR of the athletes body (Verkhoshansky 24 - 27, Verkhoshansky, Viru, 28, 286)." It "has already outlived the period of the 'orientational reflex' from the side of specialists and is finding wider use in sports practice" (PDF 555 / p.544).
- **Second way.** "tied in with the mechanism of short term adaptation. It is definitely related to such organizational-time forms of constructing the training process such as the microcycle, training day and training seance" (PDF 556 / p.545).

Both "have priority significance." "The first of them has already received plenty of substantial evaluation. The second is not considered as only a single study - even though it is sufficiently prospective," and the work relevant to it is mainly biochemical (Viru and Kirge, Viru, Verkhoshansky, Bereznoy, Dahnovsky et al, Eepik, Eepik and Viru, Osoliny et al, Usik et al) (PDF 556 / p.545).

Footnote 18 (unsigned, PDF 556 / p.545) defines the smallest unit: "A training seance or TS (from the French 'seance', the interval of time covering the non-interrupted performance of work or process in training session) ) is the form of rationalizing a one-time portion of the training load, intended to achieve one specific target (to improve the athletes' sportsmanship tactics and strategy or special physical training)." The doubled bracket is as printed.

**Why it works** — Each route is matched to one time scale of adaptation: the large cycle to compensatory, CAR-spending adaptation over weeks to months, and the session-level forms to short-term (homeostatic, restitution) adaptation over hours to days. Inference: this mirrors the two levels of the constructive effect given earlier in 9.1 (session supercompensation and the long-term delayed training effect).

**When to apply** — Inference: when auditing a plan, check both scales separately. The block level asks whether the large cycle spends and restores CAR in order; the session level asks whether each seance has one stated target, as footnote 18 requires.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a programme statement with citations to Verkhoshansky's own books; the claim that the large cycle "is finding wider use in sports practice" has no evidence on the page. He himself says the short-term route is not yet well studied. The footnote's "one specific target" is a definition, not a tested rule; a team-sport practice usually mixes targets in one session. Inference: in that setting read "seance" as one uninterrupted portion of work inside a practice, which is what the French gloss describes.

**Example** — Footnote 18's own targets for a seance: to improve "sportsmanship tactics and strategy or special physical training," one per seance (PDF 556 / p.545).

**Related** — [[framework--pasm-laws-of-adaptation-to-temporal-forms-of-training-fig-3]] (Fig 3, where the "Training seance" is the lowest time form), [[framework--large-training-cycle-local-spp-before-competition-speed-fig-14]], [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]], [[principle--mesocycle-not-microcycle-as-the-unit-and-planned-dips-are-not-errors]], [[framework--cv-and-nm-load-sequence-across-large-cycle-stages-fig-17]]

Batch 9c is done: 13 new entries written, all rated untested, and the lint is clean on every 9c file.

- **Entries:** 13 new entries.
  - **By kind:** 5 claim, 5 framework, 2 principle, 1 heuristic.
  - **By confidence:** 13 untested, none proven, supported or contested. Nothing in this range shows data, only schematic figures and citations, which matches how 9a and 9b rated the same kind of material. On PDF 561 the paper says restoration should be sped up with massage and hydro procedures, which runs against the warning on PDF 531 that clearing metabolites blunts the training effect. I treated the PDF 561 advice as Yakovlev's view, reported by Verkhoshansky, not as Verkhoshansky contradicting himself. So I recorded it as a difference and did not mark it contested.
- **Cross-links:** 18 existing entries were edited.
  - 9 got "Also in 9.1" text: 5 new lines and 4 extended lines. Unsigned footnote 21 (the meaning of "sport form" drifting from Prokop's "readiness") went into the existing Prokop sports-form entry as an Also-in line instead of a new entry.
  - The other 9 got a Related link only.
  - Every new link was confirmed on disk afterwards, because another writer was editing some of the same files at the same time.
- **Scope file:** `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/_scope_supertraining_ch9c.txt`. It lists the 13 new filenames, a blank line, then the 18 cross-linked existing entries.
- **_book.md:** I added the "9.1 (part c)" row after part b, set to done, 13 entries, printed 542-562 / PDF 553-573. `git diff` shows that one added line and no other change.
- **Exact end point:** PDF 562 / p.551, the last sentence of 9.1: "Today it is necessary to have scientific erudition and experimental-theoretical unification to seriously resolve this problem." PDF 563-573 / pp.552-562 is the 9.1 bibliography (references 1-300, Russian then non-Russian), so it was not atomized. The 9.2 Shock Method starts on PDF 574, so the batch range and 9d's start both stand.
- **Boundaries:** none moved.
  - The 1.10 heading sits mid-page on PDF 553 / p.542, as the 9b review said. Batch 9c starts there.
  - Sub-headings confirmed on the rendered pages: CONCLUSIONS and "Applied aspects of the problem" on PDF 555, and "Further perspectives in the use of the theory of adaptation in sports practice" on PDF 559.
- **Unreadable pages:** none. All pages 553-573 were rendered at 150 dpi to `staging/_renders/r9c_p<idx>.png`, and Figs 15, 16 and 17 also at 220 dpi as crops. Two pages needed care, and both were read from the image:
  - **Fig 15 (PDF 554):** text from the facing page shows through. The spans of its three brackets are my best reading and are flagged as such in the entry.
  - **PDF 557:** the right margin is tight but nothing is lost.
- **Lint:** the command as given returned `TOTAL ISSUES: 0`, but that run checks nothing: from the repo root the relative path matches no files. I ran it again with the full path (`staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky`): 0 issues in the 13 new and 18 edited entries. It reports 1 issue in `_book.md`, em dashes on lines 12, 174 and 175, which were already in the file. 9c did not add them, so I left them.
